title: Pentedatelo, Calabria, Italy

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. James Gordon Douglas III, 2014

altText: A watercolor over pencil of a place in Calabria, southern Italy, showing buildings set in a rugged landscape. The colors are soft and earthy, and pencil lines can be seen beneath the paint.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Buildings, Landscapes), classification, and image URLs read from the record

context: A watercolor over graphite by Edward Lear, the English artist and writer (1812–1888) also famous for his nonsense verse. The Met's record gives the place as Pentedatelo in Calabria, Italy, and dates the sheet 1847 with a question mark, so the date is not certain.

descriptions.k: This picture shows a place in southern Italy. There are buildings in a wild, rocky landscape. The artist used soft paint and pencil. Can you find the buildings? How do you think it feels to be there?
descriptions.g12: Edward Lear painted this place in Calabria, in southern Italy. You can see buildings and land around them. He drew with pencil first and then added watercolor. Lear also wrote funny poems! What do you think it would be like to walk through this place?
descriptions.g35: Edward Lear was an English artist who traveled to many places and painted what he saw. He is also famous for his silly poems. This watercolor over pencil shows Pentedatelo, a place in Calabria, Italy, with buildings and landscape. The date has a question mark because experts are not sure of it. What can the pencil lines and colors tell you about how Lear worked outdoors?
descriptions.g68: Lear was a traveling landscape painter who sketched places across Europe and the Mediterranean, then made watercolors from his drawings. This sheet shows Pentedatelo in Calabria, a region of southern Italy. The date in the record is 1847 with a question mark, so scholars are not certain. Notice the graphite lines under the paint. How does a travel picture work as both a memory and a record?
descriptions.g910: In this watercolor of Pentedatelo, Lear combines graphite drawing with transparent washes to describe a built place within its landscape. Lear, known to many readers as a writer of nonsense verse, was also a skilled topographical painter who traveled widely. The Met's record gives the date as 1847 with a question mark, a reminder that attribution of dates is sometimes uncertain. Consider how the sheet balances accurate description of a site with a personal sense of its character.
descriptions.g1112: Lear's view of Pentedatelo belongs to the tradition of nineteenth-century topographical watercolor, in which artists traveled to less visited places and recorded them for collectors, publishers, and themselves. The Met's date, 1847 with a query, signals scholarly caution. The combination of graphite and watercolor shows both the on-site drawing and the studio-like finish. Consider how the picture serves as evidence of a place, how it reflects an English traveler's eye on southern Italy, and what such views can and cannot tell us.

teacherNote.context: Edward Lear (1812–1888) was an English artist and writer, famous both for nonsense verse and for travel landscapes. The Met's date, 1847 with a question mark, shows that the date is uncertain.
directions: Have students sketch a place in school in pencil first and then add thin watercolor, keeping pencil visible.
Discuss why a date may be uncertain and what kinds of evidence historians use to place a work in time.
Compare a travel drawing with a photograph of the same kind of place.
